chunks.heading: Scalars vs. vectors
chunks.body: A scalar is just a size with a unit, like 10 seconds. A vector is a size and a unit plus a direction, like 10 metres north.
chunks.checkText: What does a vector have that a scalar doesn't?

chunks.heading: Drawing vectors as arrows
chunks.body: A vector can be drawn as an arrow. Its length stands for how big the vector is, and the direction it points shows the vector's direction.

chunks.heading: Using plus and minus for direction
chunks.body: When motion is along one line, one direction is labelled positive and the opposite direction is labelled negative, so numbers alone can show direction.
chunks.checkText: A negative sign on a 1D vector means it points...

chunks.heading: Adding vectors along a line
chunks.body: To combine vectors on the same line, give each one a sign using the [[phys-1d-sign-convention|sign convention]], then add the signed numbers together.

checkOptions.text: Give each vector a sign, then add

chunks.heading: Subtracting one vector from another
chunks.body: To subtract a vector, flip its direction to the opposite sign, then add it to the other vector as usual.

chunks.heading: Distance travelled
chunks.body: Distance travelled is the total length of the path something moves along. It's a scalar, and it only ever adds up, never goes down.
chunks.checkText: Distance travelled is a...

chunks.heading: Displacement
chunks.body: Displacement is how far an object's final position is from where it started, in a straight line, including the direction. It's a vector, unlike [[phys-distance-travelled|distance travelled]].
chunks.checkText: Displacement is best described as an object's...

chunks.heading: Speed
chunks.body: Speed tells you how fast [[phys-distance-travelled|distance]] is being covered. It's a scalar, so it only needs a size, no direction.
chunks.checkText: Speed is a measure of how fast...

chunks.heading: Velocity
chunks.body: Velocity tells you how fast [[phys-displacement|displacement]] is changing. Because direction matters, velocity is a vector, unlike [[phys-speed|speed]].
chunks.checkText: Unlike speed, velocity always needs a stated...

chunks.heading: Average speed
chunks.body: Average speed is the total [[phys-distance-travelled|distance travelled]] divided by the total time taken. It doesn't tell you if the speed changed along the way.
chunks.checkText: Average speed is calculated as...

checkOptions.text: Distance travelled divided by time taken

chunks.heading: Average velocity
chunks.body: Average velocity is [[phys-displacement|displacement]] divided by the time taken. If an object ends up back where it started, its average velocity is zero.
chunks.checkText: Average velocity is calculated as...

chunks.heading: One moment vs. the whole trip
chunks.body: Instantaneous speed or velocity is how fast something is moving right now, like on a speedometer. Average speed or velocity looks at the whole trip instead.
chunks.checkText: A speedometer reading shows an object's...

checkOptions.text: Average speed over the whole trip

chunks.heading: Change in speed
chunks.body: Change in speed is simply the final speed minus the initial speed. Since [[phys-speed|speed]] is a scalar, this is just plain subtraction.
chunks.checkText: To find the change in speed, you...

checkOptions.text: Subtract initial speed from final speed

chunks.heading: Change in velocity
chunks.body: Change in velocity is the final [[phys-velocity|velocity]] minus the initial velocity. Because velocity is a vector, this subtraction must account for direction.
chunks.checkText: Change in velocity must take into account...

checkOptions.text: Direction, since velocity is a vector

chunks.heading: What is acceleration?
chunks.body: Acceleration measures how quickly [[phys-velocity|velocity]] is changing. An object accelerates whenever it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.
chunks.checkText: Acceleration happens whenever an object...

checkOptions.text: Speeds up, slows down, or changes direction
Moves at a constant speed in a straight line

chunks.heading: Average acceleration
chunks.body: Average acceleration is the [[phys-change-in-velocity|change in velocity]] divided by the time it took for that change to happen.
chunks.checkText: Average acceleration is calculated as...

checkOptions.text: Change in velocity divided by time taken
Change in speed divided by distance
Final velocity divided by initial velocity

chunks.heading: What negative acceleration means
chunks.body: If the positive direction is the direction of travel, a negative [[phys-acceleration-concept|acceleration]] means an object is slowing down, not necessarily moving backwards.
chunks.checkText: If positive is the direction of travel, a negative acceleration usually means the object is...

checkOptions.text: Speeding up in the same direction

chunks.heading: Position-time graphs
chunks.body: A position-time graph plots an object's position on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, showing where it is at every moment.
chunks.checkText: A position-time graph shows an object's...

checkOptions.text: Position at each moment in time
Speed at each moment in time

chunks.heading: The slope tells you the velocity
chunks.body: The gradient (steepness) of a [[phys-position-time-graph|position-time graph]] equals the object's velocity. A flat line means the object isn't moving.
chunks.checkText: The gradient of a position-time graph gives you the object's...

chunks.heading: When the position-time graph curves
chunks.body: A curved [[phys-position-time-graph|position-time graph]] means the velocity is changing. The steepness at any single point gives the velocity at that instant.
chunks.checkText: A curved position-time graph means the object's velocity is...

chunks.heading: Velocity-time graphs
chunks.body: A velocity-time graph plots an object's velocity on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis.
chunks.checkText: A velocity-time graph shows how an object's velocity...

chunks.heading: The area under the graph is displacement
chunks.body: The area between a [[phys-velocity-time-graph|velocity-time graph]] and the time axis equals the object's displacement during that time.
chunks.checkText: The area under a velocity-time graph gives you the...

chunks.heading: The slope of a velocity-time graph
chunks.body: The gradient of a [[phys-velocity-time-graph|velocity-time graph]] equals the object's acceleration. A steeper line means a bigger acceleration.
chunks.checkText: The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives you the object's...

chunks.heading: Finding total distance from a v-t graph
chunks.body: To find total distance from a [[phys-velocity-time-graph|velocity-time graph]], add up all the areas as positive values, even the ones below the time axis.
chunks.checkText: To find total distance travelled from a velocity-time graph, you should treat all areas as...

checkOptions.text: Positive, regardless of position on the graph
Negative if below the time axis
Zero if the line is flat

chunks.heading: Acceleration-time graphs
chunks.body: An acceleration-time graph plots acceleration against time. The area under this graph equals the change in velocity over that time.
chunks.checkText: The area under an acceleration-time graph equals the...

chunks.heading: The five motion letters
chunks.body: Motion problems with steady acceleration use five values: displacement (s), initial velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), and time (t).
chunks.checkText: In the standard motion equations, the letter 'u' stands for...

chunks.heading: Equation: v = u + a*t
chunks.body: This equation finds the final velocity: v = u + a*t. Start with the initial velocity and add on however much the [[phys-acceleration-concept|acceleration]] changes it over time t.
chunks.checkText: The equation v = u + a*t is used to find the...

chunks.heading: Equation: s = ((u+v)/2)*t
chunks.body: When acceleration is steady, displacement equals the average of the initial and final velocity, multiplied by time: s = ((u+v)/2)*t.
chunks.checkText: The equation s = ((u+v)/2)*t works because, with steady acceleration, average velocity equals...

checkOptions.text: The average of initial and final velocity

chunks.heading: Equation: s = u*t + (1/2)*a*t^2
chunks.body: This equation finds displacement without needing the final velocity: s = u*t + (1/2)*a*t^2, using only the initial velocity, acceleration, and time.
chunks.checkText: The equation s = u*t + (1/2)*a*t^2 lets you find displacement without knowing the...

chunks.heading: Equation: v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s
chunks.body: This equation connects velocity and displacement without needing time: v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s. It's useful when time isn't given in a problem.
chunks.checkText: The equation v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s is especially useful when a problem doesn't give you the...

chunks.heading: Falling objects speed up the same way
chunks.body: If air resistance is ignored, all falling objects near Earth speed up at exactly the same rate, no matter how heavy or light they are.
chunks.checkText: Ignoring air resistance, a heavy object and a light object dropped together will...

chunks.heading: How fast gravity speeds things up
chunks.body: Near Earth's surface, gravity gives falling objects an [[phys-acceleration-concept|acceleration]] of about 9.8 metres per second, per second, straight down.
chunks.checkText: The acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface is about...

chunks.heading: Using the same equations for falling objects
chunks.body: The same [[phys-suvat-variables|motion equations]] used for straight-line motion also work for objects falling or thrown up, as long as you pick up or down as positive.
chunks.checkText: To use the motion equations for vertical motion, you first need to...

checkOptions.text: Choose whether up or down is positive

chunks.heading: The top of the throw
chunks.body: When something is thrown straight up, its velocity drops to exactly zero for an instant at its highest point, before it starts falling back down.
chunks.checkText: At the very top of its flight, an object thrown upward has a velocity of...

checkOptions.text: The same as when it was thrown

chunks.heading: Describing direction in two dimensions
chunks.body: On a flat plane, a vector's direction needs an angle measured from a known reference, like north, because there are far more than two possible directions.
chunks.checkText: Why does a 2D vector need an angle to describe its direction?

checkOptions.text: Because there are many possible directions, not just two
Because 2D vectors don't have a size
Because angles are easier to draw

chunks.heading: True bearings
chunks.body: A true bearing gives direction as an angle measured clockwise from north, from 0 to 360 degrees. For example, due east is 90 degrees.
chunks.checkText: A true bearing is always measured...

chunks.heading: Adding 2D vectors by drawing
chunks.body: To add vectors in two dimensions, draw them head to tail to scale, then measure the length and angle of the resultant with a ruler and protractor.
chunks.checkText: When adding vectors graphically, the resultant vector is drawn from...

checkOptions.text: The tail of the first vector to the head of the last
The head of the first vector to its own tail

chunks.heading: Adding perpendicular vectors precisely
chunks.body: For two vectors at right angles, use Pythagoras' theorem to find the resultant's size, and trigonometry to find its angle — this is more accurate than drawing.
chunks.checkText: For two vectors at right angles, Pythagoras' theorem is used to find the resultant vector's...

chunks.heading: Subtracting vectors in two dimensions
chunks.body: To subtract one 2D vector from another, reverse the direction of the vector being subtracted, then add the two vectors head to tail as usual.
chunks.checkText: To subtract a 2D vector, you first...

chunks.heading: Splitting a vector into two
chunks.body: Any vector can be split into two components at right angles to each other, which add back together to make the original vector.
chunks.checkText: The two components of a vector are always...

checkOptions.text: At right angles to each other

chunks.heading: Components can't be bigger than the original
chunks.body: Because the original vector forms the longest side of a right-angled triangle, each of its [[phys-vector-components|components]] must be smaller than the original vector.
chunks.checkText: Compared to the original vector, each of its components is always...

chunks.heading: Finding components with sine and cosine
chunks.body: To find a vector's [[phys-vector-components|components]], multiply its size by cosine of the angle for one component, and by sine of the angle for the other.
chunks.checkText: To calculate a vector's components, you multiply its magnitude by...

checkOptions.text: Sine and cosine of the angle

chunks.heading: Frame of reference
chunks.body: A frame of reference is the point or object you're measuring motion from. Motion can look different depending on whether that point is still or moving.
chunks.checkText: A frame of reference is best described as...

checkOptions.text: The point motion is measured from

chunks.heading: Finding velocity relative to another object
chunks.body: To find object A's velocity relative to object B, using a stationary [[phys-frame-of-reference|reference]] C, add A's velocity relative to C to C's velocity relative to B.
chunks.checkText: To find the velocity of A relative to B via a reference point C, you...

checkOptions.text: Add A relative to C, and C relative to B

chunks.heading: Reversing a relative velocity
chunks.body: The velocity of A relative to B is always the exact opposite of the velocity of B relative to A.
chunks.checkText: The velocity of A relative to B compared to B relative to A is...

chunks.heading: A boat crossing a flowing river
chunks.body: A boat's velocity relative to the ground equals its velocity relative to the water, added to the water's own velocity relative to the ground.
chunks.checkText: A boat's velocity relative to the ground is found by adding its velocity relative to the water to the...

checkOptions.text: Water's velocity relative to the ground
Boat's top speed in still water

chunks.heading: A plane flying through wind
chunks.body: A plane's velocity relative to the ground equals its velocity relative to the wind, added to the wind's own velocity relative to the ground — just like a [[phys-boat-river-relative-motion|boat crossing a river]].
chunks.checkText: A plane's velocity relative to the ground is found by adding its velocity relative to the wind to the...

checkOptions.text: Wind's velocity relative to the ground
